That is why Llama 3 forecast accuracy through NLL first. It does not prove no real change ever happens, but the jump alone is not evidence of one.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Average precision, MAP and MRR: one number for a whole ranking
question: You evaluate a search box that jumps the user straight to a product page (each query has exactly one correct product). Which metric best matches the user's experience?
options: MRR
Recall@1000
MAP over all relevant products
11-point interpolated precision
explain: With exactly one right answer, what matters is how high it appears, which is what reciprocal rank measures. Recall@1000 ignores position. With a single relevant document AP equals RR anyway, and the recall-level machinery of 11-point precision adds nothing.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
question: You must rank 1,000,000 passages for each incoming query. Which cost profile describes a pure cross-encoder versus a bi-encoder at query time?
options: Both need 1,000,000 forward passes per query; the bi-encoder just uses a smaller model
Cross-encoder: 1,000,000 forward passes per query. Bi-encoder: 1 forward pass for the query plus 1,000,000 vector similarities
Cross-encoder: 1 forward pass per query. Bi-encoder: 1,000,000 forward passes
Both need 1 forward pass, because attention handles all passages at once
explain: The cross-encoder has to read the query together with every passage, so its work scales with the corpus on every query. The bi-encoder encoded the passages offline; online it encodes only the query and then does cheap dot products, which an index can speed up further.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Modern training: web pairs, mined negatives and distillation
question: E5-mistral is a decoder-only LLM. Why does it take the vector at the final [EOS] token instead of averaging all token vectors?
options: Averaging is too slow for a 7-billion-parameter model
Causal attention lets each token see only earlier tokens, so only the last position has seen the whole text
The [EOS] vector is always longer than the others
Mean pooling cannot be normalized
explain: In a decoder, early tokens never see later ones, so their vectors summarize only a prefix. The last position has attended to everything. Speed and normalization have nothing to do with it.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
question: Re-ranking costs about 0.78 s for 100 candidates on your CPU, and your latency budget for this stage is 200 ms. What is the most direct way to fit it?
options: Re-rank 1,000 candidates in one batch, which is faster per pair
Remove the bi-encoder stage
Re-rank fewer candidates (about 20), since cost grows linearly with the candidate count
Use a larger cross-encoder
explain: Each candidate is one forward pass, so 20 candidates cost about a fifth of 100. On SciFact, re-ranking the top 20 kept most of the gain (0.680 vs 0.682 nDCG@10). More candidates or a bigger model cost more, and without a first stage there is nothing to re-rank.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Encoding new text: replay the merges in rank order
question: A teammate's encoder, given lowest, first merges (l, o) because l o is the leftmost pair present in the merge list. Is the final result different here, and what is the bug?
options: Different result; the merge list should be applied left to right
Same result here, but the rule is wrong: merges must be applied by lowest rank, and on other inputs left to right gives splits the model never saw
Same result, and the rule is fine since merges commute
Different result; BPE merges the most frequent pair in the current word
explain: For lowest both orders happen to end at low est_. But BPE's contract is rank order: the encoder must reproduce the segmentation used during training. Merges do not commute in general (merging one pair can destroy an overlapping one), so a left-to-right encoder can disagree with the model's training data on other inputs.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Tradeoffs: vocab size, numbers, languages, glitch tokens, alternatives
question: A team moves a code assistant from the GPT-2 tokenizer to cl100k_base. On their Python files bytes per token goes from about 2 to about 4. Which effect should they expect, with the model's context window unchanged in tokens?
options: No change, because the text is the same number of bytes
Each file costs fewer tokens, and the embedding table also shrinks because tokens are longer
Each file costs more tokens, because a bigger vocabulary means longer ids
About twice as much code fits in the same context, and each file needs about half as many positions to process; the cost is a vocabulary about twice as large
explain: Doubling bytes per token halves the tokens for the same bytes, so about twice as much code fits in the window and about half as many positions are processed. The table does not shrink: it has one row per vocabulary entry, so it grows from 50,257 to about 100k rows, in the embedding and in the output layer.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Optimizers: momentum, Adam and decoupled weight decay
question: You switch from `torch.optim.Adam(params, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01)` to `torch.optim.AdamW(params, lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01)`. What changes?
options: Nothing; the two classes are aliases
Decay is now applied directly as w -= lr x 0.01 x w, instead of being added to the gradient and rescaled by 1/sqrt(v)
AdamW disables bias correction
AdamW applies decay only to biases
explain: Adam's weight_decay adds lambda x w to the gradient, which then passes through the m/sqrt(v) ratio. AdamW shrinks the weights in a separate step, so every weight decays at the rate lr x lambda regardless of its gradient history.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm and dropout: train vs eval mode
question: You train a model whose batches have only 2 examples per GPU and see unstable results. Which normalization is the natural fix?
options: BatchNorm with momentum 0.01
LayerNorm, since its statistics come from each example alone
Increase dropout to 0.9
Remove the learned gamma and beta
explain: Batch statistics from 2 examples are extremely noisy. LayerNorm's mean and variance are computed over one example's features, so batch size does not matter. The LayerNorm paper names batch-size dependence as the limitation it was designed to remove.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: Why exact nearest-neighbor search stops scaling
question: Your collection grows from 1 million to 4 million vectors and you upgrade to a machine with 2x the memory bandwidth. Under the linear-scan model, what happens to brute-force latency?
options: It doubles: 4x the data over 2x the bandwidth
It stays the same, because the bandwidth doubled
It quadruples, because bandwidth does not affect latency
It halves, because more bandwidth beats more data
explain: Brute force reads every vector, so time scales with N divided by bandwidth: 4 / 2 = 2x slower. Hardware gives constant factors; the linear growth in N remains.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: HNSW, IVF, PQ and production indexes
lessonTitle: IVF: clustering the space, nlist and nprobe
question: You build an IVF index with nlist = 4,096. Following Faiss's guideline, how large should the k-means training sample be?
options: Between about 123,000 and 1 million vectors (30 to 256 per centroid)
At least 4,096 vectors, one per centroid
Exactly 64 vectors, the square root of 4,096
None: the inverted lists are built without training
explain: Faiss asks for between 30 x K and 256 x K training vectors for K centroids: 30 x 4,096 = 122,880 and 256 x 4,096 = 1,048,576. One vector per centroid gives k-means nothing to average, and IVF, unlike HNSW, cannot be built without training.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: The software supply chain: a map with every attack point
question: Why do attackers bother compromising a build server or a popular library instead of attacking their real targets directly?
options: It is legal to modify open source code
One compromise fans out to every downstream user, through channels they already trust
Libraries are never scanned by antivirus
Build servers have weaker passwords than anything else
explain: Fan-out and trust: SolarWinds' signed update reached its customers' networks through the normal update channel, with no exploit needed at each victim.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Maintainer takeover: when the real publisher ships malware
question: Why could Shai-Hulud spread from package to package without a human attacker choosing each target?
options: Each infected developer's own npm credentials let it publish infected versions of that developer's other packages
It relied on dependency confusion
It used typosquatted names
It exploited a bug in the npm registry
explain: That is what makes it a worm: the stolen credentials of each victim become the delivery channel to the next set of packages. Short-lived, CI-only publishing credentials break the loop.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: GitHub Actions attacks: pwn requests, injection and moving tags
question: Why did pinning tj-actions/changed-files to a full commit SHA protect users when pinning to v45.0.7 did not?
options: A commit SHA identifies exact content; moving it would need a SHA-1 collision, while a tag is a pointer anyone with write access can move
Version tags are deleted after 30 days
SHAs are secret, so attackers cannot guess them
GitHub scans SHA-pinned actions for malware
explain: This is GitHub's own rationale. Pinning swaps 'whatever this tag means today' for 'exactly this content', which is the same idea as a lockfile.

courseTitle: Software supply chain security
lessonTitle: Scanning dependencies: OSV, advisories and Dependabot
question: Dependabot opens no pull request for a malware alert on a package you use. Why?
options: The alert is a false positive
Dependabot ignores npm packages
Malware advisories have no fixed version to upgrade to; the safe action is to remove or replace the package and investigate
Malware alerts require a paid plan
explain: GitHub's docs: malware alerts do not contain a fix version, because there are no safe versions of the malicious package. You remove it and treat affected machines as compromised.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Why resampling your own outputs erases rare events
question: A token's fitted probability hits exactly 0 at generation 4 of this fully synthetic loop. What is the chance it reappears at generation 50?
options: About its original probability, because errors average out over generations
Small but positive, because sampling is random
Zero, because a token with probability 0 is never sampled and refitting cannot invent it
About 1/M, because each generation draws M fresh samples
explain: The histogram model can only assign mass to tokens it has seen. Once a count is zero the token has probability zero, so no later sample contains it. Only an outside source of real data could bring it back.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Replace versus accumulate: what keeps the error bounded
question: A lab keeps all its human text and, every year, adds model-written text so that a steady 20% of the mix is synthetic, from generators whose outputs differ systematically from human text. It then scales the total data tenfold. Which prediction fits the results in this lesson best?
options: Test error diverges, as in the replace loop
Test error keeps falling as a power law, because real data are never thrown away
The model collapses to a point mass within a few generations
Test error stops improving at a floor set by the synthetic share and its mismatch, but does not diverge
explain: Real data are kept, so this is not the replace setting and nothing diverges. But a fixed, non-vanishing share of mismatched data adds a floor of about p2^2 c^2 (strong model collapse): a change in the scaling law, which is one of the eight definitions Schaeffer et al. list.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When a system call blocks: sleeping, short counts and EINTR
question: A server sends a 1 MB response with `if (write(sock, buf, 1000000) == -1) die();` on a non-blocking socket. Clients sometimes receive truncated responses but the server logs no error. Why?
options: The kernel splits large writes into packets and some packets are lost
write returned -1 with EAGAIN, which die() ignored
write returned a short count, fewer than 1,000,000 bytes, and the code never sent the rest
Sockets need fsync before the data is sent
explain: A non-blocking socket accepts only what fits in its send buffer and returns that count. The check only catches -1, so the rest of the buffer is silently never sent. The fix is a write_all style loop that advances by the returned count and waits for writability (for example with epoll) on EAGAIN. TCP itself retransmits lost packets, so loss is not the cause.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: Shared memory between processes: MAP_SHARED, shm_open and memfd
question: A parent wants to read a result its child writes after fork. Which setup makes the child's write visible to the parent?
options: malloc a buffer before fork
mmap with MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS before fork
mmap with MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS in the child after fork
mmap with MAP_SHARED | MAP_ANONYMOUS before fork
explain: Only a shared mapping that exists before fork is inherited by the child with the same attributes, so both point at the same pages. malloc memory and MAP_PRIVATE mappings are copy-on-write after fork, so the child's write lands in its own copy. A mapping created in the child after fork exists only in the child.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Coordinated omission: the load tester stops looking when it hurts
question: Which change to a closed-loop tester does NOT fix coordinated omission?
options: Measuring each request from the time the schedule says it should have been sent
Sending requests on a fixed schedule from independent senders that never wait for responses
Adding more connections so that each one blocks less often
Back-filling the missing samples using a known expected interval between requests
explain: More connections reduce the effect but every connection still stops sending while it waits, so the bias remains (the NSDI paper notes closed systems approach open ones only slowly as concurrency grows). Measuring from intended start, open-loop sending, and interval-based back-fill all restore the missing samples.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: SS7: a signalling club that stopped being a club
question: A location query about one of your subscribers arrives from a Global Title that belongs to a real foreign operator. Why is that not enough to trust it?
options: Global Titles are encrypted, so you cannot read them
Foreign operators are never allowed to send any SS7 message
Location queries are always sent by the subscriber's own phone
SS7 access is leased and resold, and SS7 identifiers are not authenticated, so a real operator's GT does not prove a legitimate sender or purpose
explain: ENISA notes SS7 access can be bought and that SS7 identifiers can be spoofed. Foreign operators do legitimately send many messages (roaming needs them), so a blanket ban is wrong; the question is whether this message type, about this subscriber, makes sense from that source.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: IMSI catchers and false base stations: downgrade and detection
question: Why can a false base station not simply impersonate a 4G network all the way through to intercepting calls?
options: 4G masts have unique colours that phones check
4G phones never send any messages before authentication
4G AKA makes the phone verify a MAC that only the home network (which knows K) can produce, so the false station pushes the phone to 2G instead
4G uses satellites instead of masts
explain: AKA authenticates the network to the phone, so a false 4G station cannot complete authentication. That is why downgrade to 2G, where the network is never authenticated, is the common route. Some messages are still exchanged before authentication in 4G, which Shaik et al. exploited for location leaks and denial of service.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: SIM swaps and port-outs: an identity problem, not a radio problem
question: A bank's fraud check says the customer's number had a SIM swap 6 hours ago, and the customer is now asking to add a new payee. What should the bank do?
options: Send an SMS code to confirm, since SMS is a second factor
Hold or step up with a factor not tied to the number, such as a registered passkey, or call back on independently known details
Approve it, because the password was correct
Ask the customer to reply STOP
explain: Right after a SIM swap the SMS channel may be controlled by the attacker, so an SMS code proves nothing. NIST lists SIM change as a risk indicator before using the phone channel, and the ITU report recommends exactly this timing check.

courseTitle: Telecom and satellite security: SS7, SIM swapping, 5G and space links
lessonTitle: Case: the Viasat KA-SAT attack (24 February 2022)
question: Which statement best matches Viasat's account of how the modems were disabled?
options: Legitimate management commands, sent from inside the management network after a VPN misconfiguration was exploited, overwrote data in the modems' flash memory
Malicious firmware was pushed through the normal update server
The satellite was hacked from space
Users downloaded malware onto their PCs
explain: Viasat found no evidence its firmware distribution or update processes were used, and no evidence the satellite or ground infrastructure itself was compromised. The destructive step travelled over normal management functionality, reached through a misconfigured VPN appliance; it ran a wiper on the modems rather than replacing their firmware.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Why summing job durations overstates experience
question: A candidate has two roles: Jan 2020 to Dec 2022 full-time and Jan 2021 to Dec 2021 part-time (both inclusive). A filter asks for 4+ years of experience. What should happen?
options: Match: 36 + 12 = 48 months is exactly 4 years
No match: the union is 36 months, 3 years
Match, because part-time roles always count double
It cannot be decided without the LLM
explain: The part-time role lies entirely inside the full-time one, so the union is Jan 2020 to Dec 2022, 36 months. Summing gives 48 months only because 2021 is counted twice.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Let the LLM parse and let code do the date math
question: Why does `date(2023, 1, 31) + relativedelta(months=1)` return 2023-02-28 instead of raising an error or returning March 3?
options: relativedelta clamps to the last valid day: adding months never crosses a month boundary
It adds 28 days
It converts the date to a timestamp and adds 30 days
February 29 is skipped in non-leap years by adding 29 days
explain: The dateutil docs state that adding a month never crosses the month boundary, so day 31 is clamped to the last day of February. That is the calendar-month semantics you want for *Sep 2021 plus 3 years* style questions.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Verifiers set the ceiling: error rates, GenRM and self-verification
question: After filtering, AlphaCode still has 2,000 programs that pass the example tests and only 10 submissions. Why pick one program from each of the largest behavior clusters?
options: Large clusters contain the shortest programs
Clustering runs the hidden tests in advance
Programs with identical outputs are redundant submissions, and correct programs tend to agree with each other, so big clusters are more likely correct
It guarantees that one submission passes
explain: Random picks waste submissions on semantically equal programs. Grouping by behavior on new inputs spreads the 10 submissions over distinct behaviors, and the paper found that going from largest to smallest cluster worked best.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Exchanging test-time compute for a bigger model
question: Brown et al.'s DeepSeek-Coder setup beat single attempts from GPT-4o and Claude on SWE-bench Lite. Which ingredient made the extra samples convertible into solved issues?
options: A majority vote over patches
A larger context window
A process reward model
The repository's unit tests, which check each candidate automatically
explain: SWE-bench candidates are checked by the repository's test suite, so higher coverage becomes a higher solve rate directly. Without such a checker, selection plateaus, as lesson 3 showed.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Making TTT fast: mini-batch gradient descent and the dual form
question: What does the dual form change about a TTT layer?
options: Its outputs: it is an approximation that trades accuracy for speed
Only how the same outputs are computed: matmuls replace per-token outer products, and the intermediate G_t and W_t are never stored
The loss: it switches from reconstruction to a dot-product loss
The order of updates: it processes tokens right to left
explain: The paper stresses that primal and dual forms are equivalent in output. The dual form spends a bit more theoretical compute (an extra O(b^2 d) term) to get matmul-friendly operations and avoid materializing b matrices of size d x d.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Large-chunk TTT, one map of the design space, and the costs
question: You build a LaCT language model with 2048-token chunks and apply-then-update ordering, but you delete the window attention to save compute. What breaks?
options: Nothing; the fast weights still see every earlier token
Within a chunk, a token's TTT output only reflects earlier chunks, so tokens cannot use their nearby chunk-mates through the TTT layer
Future tokens leak into the past, so training loss looks too good
The model becomes quadratic in sequence length
explain: With apply-then-update, all queries in a chunk read the weights from the end of the previous chunk. That prevents leakage but means up to 2047 preceding tokens in the same chunk are invisible to the TTT layer. LaCT adds local window attention exactly to cover that within-chunk context.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
question: CPU 2 only frees packet buffers; CPU 5 only allocates them. With magazines and a depot, how do buffers get from CPU 2 to CPU 5?
options: Each buffer goes back to the slab layer, then CPU 5 takes it from there
CPU 5 steals single objects from CPU 2's magazine under CPU 2's lock
CPU 2 returns full magazines to the depot and CPU 5 loads them, moving M buffers per depot visit
They cannot: each CPU's objects are private forever
explain: Whole magazines are the unit of exchange. The freeing CPU fills magazines and swaps them for empties at the depot; the allocating CPU swaps empties for those full ones. The depot lock is taken about once per M objects on each side.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: What threat hunting is, and the hunt that started at 75 cents
question: Once Stoll knew which accounts the intruder had stolen, LBL placed alarms on the incoming lines that paged an operator whenever those account names appeared. Which hunting outcome is that?
options: Escalating to incident response and ending the hunt
Turning what the hunt learned into an automated detection
Attribution of the intruder
A data gap that needs a new log source
explain: The hunt discovered something specific and reliable (the stolen account names), and the team automated watching for it, so people could spend their time on what was still unknown. Modern frameworks call this step 'create detections' (PEAK) or 'inform and enrich analytics' (Sqrrl's Hunting Loop).

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in EDR data I: process trees in KQL
question: In a DeviceProcessEvents row for a newly created `cmd.exe`, which column names the program that started it?
options: InitiatingProcessFileName
FileName
ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName
DeviceName
explain: FileName (with ProcessCommandLine) describes the new process; InitiatingProcessFileName is the process responsible for the event, here its parent. InitiatingProcessParentFileName goes one generation further up. The version-info column is the name compiled into the file, used for the renamed-tool hunt.

courseTitle: Threat hunting
lessonTitle: Hunting in identity data: what the SolarWinds intruders left
question: Your one-to-many hunt flags JUMP1 (1 account, 40 servers) and WS077 (4 accounts, 4 servers). Which deserves escalation, and why?
options: JUMP1, because 40 destinations is more
Both equally, because both exceed a threshold
Neither, because valid credentials were used
WS077, because many different accounts from one ordinary workstation is the unusual pattern; one admin account fanning out from a jump host is its purpose
explain: FireEye's opportunity was many accounts from one source, which normal business rarely produces. A jump host is designed for one admin to reach many servers, so record it as known-benign. Valid credentials are exactly what this hunt is for: the logons succeed because the attacker holds real accounts.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: What threat intelligence is, and what it is for
question: In the FIRST ladder, a rule such as: the intruder first used a backdoor beaconing to one address, then swapped it for a file with a known hash once access was established. Which level is it?
options: Knowledge (behavioural indicator)
Data (atomic indicator)
Information (computed indicator)
Not an indicator at all
explain: It combines atomic and computed indicators with sequence and logic, which is what the kill chain paper calls a behavioural indicator and FIRST maps to knowledge. It is still not intelligence until someone attaches a judgement and a recommendation for a decision.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Indicators: types, life cycle and decay
question: In MISP's Polynomial model, what happens if you raise the decay speed while keeping the same lifetime?
options: The score falls sooner within the lifetime
The indicator never decays
The lifetime doubles
The base score increases
explain: The exponent is 1/speed. A larger speed makes (t/lifetime) raised to that power approach 1 sooner, so the score drops earlier. MISP's documentation says a larger positive value 'makes the score fall sooner within the same lifetime'.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Sharing at machine speed: TAXII, MISP and communities
question: Your TAXII client polls a collection every hour. What stops it re-downloading the same objects each time?
options: Passing added_after with the time of the last successful poll, using the X-TAXII-Date-Added headers to know where to resume
Nothing: TAXII always returns the full collection
Deleting the collection after each download
Using DNS SRV records
explain: TAXII 2.1 supports an added_after URL parameter, and servers return X-TAXII-Date-Added-First and -Last headers describing the page returned. Clients resume from there. DNS SRV records are for discovering servers, not paging.

courseTitle: Cyber threat intelligence
lessonTitle: Writing an intelligence product people act on
question: Which key judgement follows FIRST's guidance on communicating uncertainty?
options: It is likely that the actor will target our VPN within 30 days. We have moderate confidence in this assessment.
We believe the actor could possibly be targeting us.
It is likely, with moderate confidence and maybe high, that the actor might target us.
The actor will definitely attack us.
explain: The correct sentence pair uses a WEP term for probability and an LCA level for confidence, in separate sentences, with a bounded time window. 'We believe ... could possibly' uses the vague words FIRST warns against; the mixed sentence piles terms into one hedge; 'definitely' claims certainty no evidence supports.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: STRIDE: six ways things go wrong
question: An attacker on café Wi-Fi reads session cookies from unencrypted HTTP traffic. Which STRIDE category is this, at the moment of reading?
options: Information disclosure
Repudiation
Tampering
Denial of service
explain: Reading data in transit that you should not see breaks confidentiality. Using the stolen cookie afterwards would be spoofing; changing the traffic would be tampering.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Design principles I: simple, closed by default, checked every time
question: A file server grants access unless the path matches a list of forbidden folders. A new folder of payroll files is created. What happens, and which principle explains it?
options: Payroll is readable until someone adds it to the list: fail-safe defaults was violated
Payroll is refused until someone grants it: complete mediation was followed
Nothing changes, because new folders inherit the parent's permissions
The server crashes: economy of mechanism was violated
explain: Exclusion-based rules fail open for anything new. Saltzer and Schroeder's point is that a permission-based rule would fail closed, and the mistake would be noticed when someone was refused.

courseTitle: Thinking like an attacker: threat models and security principles
lessonTitle: Who do you trust? Thompson's compiler and SolarWinds
question: Thompson's bugged compiler has been rebuilt from clean source many times. Why does reading the compiler's source code not reveal the backdoor?
options: The backdoor exists only in the compiler binary, which re-inserts it whenever it compiles the compiler
The source is encrypted
The backdoor is in the login source code
Compilers cannot be inspected
explain: Stage III moves the bug out of the source and into the binary, which reproduces it in each new compiler. The login source is clean too; the binary compiler adds the backdoor when it compiles login.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Demotion: reclaim that migrates instead of swapping
question: Why does TPP keep reclaiming past the normal high watermark on the fast node?
options: To reduce the number of pages on the CXL node
Because reclaim is cheaper when done in larger batches
To make room for short-lived hot allocations and incoming promotions so they land in DRAM instead of spilling to CXL
To keep the inactive list empty
explain: New allocations go to CXL only when the local node is short of free pages. Headroom keeps those bursts local, and promotions need free local frames too. Upstream implements this with the promo watermark.

courseTitle: Time-series forecasting: baselines, smoothing and honest backtests
lessonTitle: Honest evaluation: error metrics, MASE and rolling origins
question: Sales of a niche product are 0 in some weeks. A dashboard compares models by MAPE. What goes wrong, and what is a better choice?
options: Nothing, MAPE handles zeros by skipping them
MAPE becomes negative, so use sMAPE instead
MAPE overweights large values, so use RMSE on percentages
MAPE is undefined when actuals are 0 and explodes near 0, so use a scaled metric such as MASE
explain: Percentage errors divide by $y_t$, so a zero actual makes the error infinite or undefined and small actuals dominate the average. MASE divides by the in-sample naive or seasonal naive MAE instead, which is nonzero unless the training series is constant (or, for the seasonal scale, repeats exactly every season). sMAPE is not recommended either.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: The key schedule: one shared secret, many keys
question: Why does TLS 1.3 derive separate client-to-server and server-to-client keys?
options: So that a record sent by one side can never be reflected back and accepted as coming from the other
To double the encryption strength
Because AES cannot encrypt in both directions
To let the server use a different cipher suite
explain: With one shared key an attacker could bounce a client's record back to the client, and it would decrypt correctly. Direction-specific keys make that fail. This is key separation in action.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Reading an X.509 certificate field by field
question: Which name does `*.shop.example` cover?
options: shop.example
api.shop.example
v2.api.shop.example
All three
explain: The wildcard stands for exactly one whole label on the left. It does not match the bare domain and does not span two labels (RFC 9525).

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: When CAs fail: DigiNotar, Symantec and an expired root
question: Why did some clients fail after 30 September 2021 even though they trusted ISRG Root X1?
options: ISRG Root X1 was revoked that day
Their path building (for example OpenSSL 1.0.x) chose the chain through the expired DST Root CA X3 cross-sign instead of the valid path to ISRG Root X1
Let's Encrypt changed signature algorithms
Their system clocks were wrong
explain: Two valid-looking paths existed. Modern libraries try alternatives; OpenSSL 1.0.x had a quirk that made it fail on the expired one. Path building is part of validation, and its bugs cause outages.

courseTitle: TLS and PKI in practice
lessonTitle: Mutual TLS and running your own internal CA
question: In TLS 1.3 mTLS, which message tells the client it must present a certificate?
options: ClientHello
NewSessionTicket
Finished
CertificateRequest from the server
explain: The server sends CertificateRequest after EncryptedExtensions. The client answers with Certificate and CertificateVerify before its Finished.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
question: A Triton program loads a block of 1024 floats and is compiled with num_warps=4. How many hardware threads share that block?
options: 1, because Triton programs are single-threaded
32, one warp
128, so on average 8 values per thread
1024, one per value
explain: num_warps=4 means 4 x 32 = 128 threads cooperate on one program instance. The 1024 values are spread over them, 8 per thread on average. The single-threaded view is how you write the code, not how it runs.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
question: A kernel is autotuned with key=["M", "N", "K"]. You call it 1000 times with M = N = K = 4096, then once with K = 8192. How many times does it benchmark the full config list?
options: Once, on the very first call only
Twice: on the first 4096 call and on the first call with K = 8192
1001 times, once per call
Never, configs are chosen at import time
explain: Autotuning reruns whenever the values of the key arguments change. The first 4096 call benchmarks and caches the winner, the next 999 reuse it, and the new K value triggers one more round.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Continuous images: one transformer, two losses
question: Why does capping the diffusion noise at t = 500 for image-before-caption pairs help captioning?
options: The caption tokens attend to the image, and with full noise they would often be describing near-pure noise
It halves the number of image tokens
It makes the image loss computed per token instead of per image
It switches the image to discrete tokens
explain: In training the image is noised for its own diffusion loss, and later tokens condition on that noisy version. When the caption follows the image, a heavily noised image hides the content to describe. Limiting noise keeps the image readable; the paper measured better CIDEr with under 1% effect elsewhere.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Concurrency in one address space: cooperative threads and no fork
question: Four requests arrive together at a single-vCPU cooperative event loop. Each needs 2 ms of CPU and then 3 ms of I/O wait. When does the last one finish?
options: At 8 ms, when the last handler stops computing
At 11 ms
At 20 ms, since each request takes 5 ms
At 5 ms, since all four overlap fully
explain: CPU work cannot overlap on one vCPU: handlers run at 0-2, 2-4, 4-6 and 6-8 ms. Each I/O overlaps the next handler, so the last request waits from 8 to 11 ms. A blocking single thread would take 4 x 5 = 20 ms.

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Specializing further, and what you give up
question: Which service is the weakest candidate for a unikernel?
options: A stateless HTTP API that must cold-start in milliseconds per request burst
A DNS server facing the internet where attack surface matters
A UDP packet processor that needs millions of packets per second per core
A CI build runner that shells out to compilers, git and test scripts in many child processes
explain: The build runner depends on fork, exec and many separate programs, which a single-address-space unikernel supports poorly at best: there is no copying fork, and Unikraft's vfork plus execve covers only simple spawning. The other three match unikernel strengths: fast boot, small attack surface and low-level I/O specialization.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: SIMD distance kernels: lanes, FMA and the horizontal sum
question: A colleague's AVX-512 kernel uses one accumulator and runs 768-d distances on vectors that fit in L1. Splitting it into four accumulators makes it faster. Why?
options: Four accumulators halve the number of loads
Independent accumulators let several FMAs run in parallel instead of waiting on one dependency chain
AVX-512 cannot use a single register for more than 12 FMAs
Four accumulators avoid the horizontal sum
explain: Each FMA into the same register must wait for the previous result. Four independent chains keep the FMA units busy. Loads and the final reduction are unchanged (the reduction even gets slightly longer).

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: Durability and memory tiers: WAL, mmap and disk-based ANN
question: A Qdrant point is at version 42 in a segment. During WAL replay the server sees op 40 (an upsert of that point). What happens?
options: It is applied, because replay must re-execute every logged operation
It is ignored, because its sequence number is lower than the point's current version
The segment is rebuilt from scratch
Replay stops with a corruption error
explain: The documented rule is to ignore a change whose sequential number is less than the point's current version. That makes replaying the whole log idempotent (running it again changes nothing) with respect to already-applied newer state.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: WorkerGroups, resource pools and DataProto dispatch
question: `init_model` is registered with Dispatch.ONE_TO_ALL. What does the controller send to each worker when it calls `wg.init_model()`?
options: A different slice of the arguments to each worker
The same arguments, replicated once per worker
Arguments only to rank 0, which then broadcasts them
Nothing; ONE_TO_ALL methods run on the controller process
explain: dispatch_one_to_all copies every argument world_size times, so every worker runs the same call. It suits setup methods like init_model. DP_COMPUTE_PROTO is the mode that splits a DataProto into per-worker chunks.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Backends, placement and tuning verl in practice
question: Your synchronous run's step time is dominated by a few very long responses, and the GPUs idle while waiting for them. Which verl option targets exactly this, and what does it cost?
options: Raise ppo_mini_batch_size; it costs more memory
Switch model_engine to megatron; it costs a checkpoint conversion
Lower rollout.n; it costs nothing
Overlap generation with training (one-step-off style, which the V1 trainer offers as async modes, lesson 7); training then uses samples partly generated by older weights
explain: The async modes stop waiting for the tail: stragglers keep generating, or are aborted and resumed, while training proceeds. The price is bounded staleness, which lesson 7 shows how to cap. Lowering n changes the algorithm, and mini-batch or engine changes do not touch the rollout tail.

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: Algorithms as config: critics, estimators and rollout correction
question: Which estimator costs an extra generation pass per prompt?
options: rloo
remax
reinforce_plus_plus
grpo_passk
explain: ReMax's baseline is the reward of a greedy response to the same prompt, so the trainer must generate one more response with sampling turned off. RLOO, REINFORCE++ and pass@k GRPO build their baselines from the sampled responses or the batch.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Merging similar frames: MovieChat and MA-LMM memory banks
question: A 10-minute static lecture shot is followed by a 3-second cutaway, then the lecture again. With adjacent-similarity merging down to a small budget, what most likely happens?
options: The lecture frames collapse to few tokens while the cutaway survives as its own token
The cutaway is merged first because it is shortest
All frames are merged into one token immediately
The lecture frames are deleted and only the cutaway remains
explain: Near-identical lecture frames have the highest adjacent similarity, so they merge first. The cutaway has low similarity to both neighbors, so it is merged last, if at all. Merging spends the budget on change.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Tokenizing video and attending in space, then in time
question: Why might a spatial-only tokenizer (one frame at a time) give worse controllability than ST-ViViT?
options: Its codebook is necessarily smaller
Spatial attention is more expensive than temporal attention
It uses a causal mask in space
It cannot encode information about motion between frames into the tokens
explain: A per-frame encoder sees no other frames, so its tokens carry no motion context. The ST tokenizer's causal temporal layers let each frame's tokens include what happened before, which helps the downstream models predict and control change.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: The hypervisor as a security boundary: who must not reach whom
question: In the toy, why does SGDT run without the VMM noticing while MOV_CR3 is caught?
options: SGDT is not sensitive, so the VMM does not need to see it
The VMM chose to let SGDT through for speed
MOV_CR3 is caught because it is slower than SGDT
SGDT is sensitive but not privileged, so running it deprivileged causes no trap
explain: Trap-and-emulate depends on every sensitive instruction trapping. SGDT reads machine state (sensitive) but does not fault outside ring 0 (not privileged), so it violates Popek and Goldberg's condition. Robin and Irvine found seventeen such instructions on the Pentium.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Hypervisor designs: where device models run and what one bug reaches
question: Why does a bug in a Hyper-V VSP tend to be more severe than the same bug in a QEMU device model on a well-configured KVM host?
options: The VSP runs in the root partition's kernel, while QEMU runs as a confined unprivileged process, so the QEMU bug needs a second escape
VSPs are written in an unsafe language and QEMU is not
Hyper-V has no IOMMU support
QEMU device models are never reachable from guests
explain: Both are written in C. The difference is where the code runs: kernel-side device code is already at the top, while a confined user-space device model is one sandbox away from it.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Xen: guest types, stub domains and the XSA process
question: During an XSA embargo, a cloud operator on the pre-disclosure list wants to switch every guest to stub domains, a change visible to guests. What does the XSA-133 text say?
options: Allowed: any mitigation can be deployed
Allowed only on Arm
Required before patching
Not allowed on public clouds, because the change may be visible to the guest and reveal the issue
explain: XSA-133 permitted deploying the patches, but not the stubdomain mitigation on public cloud systems, 'because this configuration change may be visible to the guest'.

courseTitle: Virtualization and hypervisor security
lessonTitle: Confidential VMs: SEV-SNP, TDX and Arm CCA stop trusting the host
question: Plain SEV encrypts each VM's memory. What attack did SEV-SNP's reverse map table add protection against?
options: Reading guest memory in plaintext
Denial of service by the host
Side channels through shared caches
The hypervisor remapping or replaying encrypted guest pages, for example mapping one page twice
explain: Encryption hides contents but not placement. A hypervisor that controls the nested page tables could swap or replay ciphertext pages. The RMP enforces one owner and one guest address per page; denial of service remains out of scope.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Where ViT-B/16's 86 million parameters live
question: You switch from 224x224 to 384x384 inputs on ViT-B/16. Which parameter tensor has to change shape?
options: Every Q, K and V matrix, because the sequence is longer
The patch projection E, because there are more patches
Only the position embedding table, from 197 x 768 to 577 x 768
None: the model handles any resolution without changes
explain: Attention and MLP weights act on each token's D-vector, so their shapes depend on D, not on sequence length. E acts on each 16x16x3 patch, unchanged. Only the learned table has one row per slot, so it must grow from 197 to 577 rows.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts
question: In Open X-Embodiment, two robots receive the identical 7-number action vector. Why might they move very differently?
options: The 256-bin tokenizer uses a different vocabulary for each robot
Actions are normalized per dataset and frames and control modes (position vs velocity, absolute vs relative) are not aligned, so the same numbers mean different motions
Open X-Embodiment stores only images, so actions are re-estimated per robot
The model adds a robot-specific noise term at inference
explain: The paper says the alignment is coarse: each dataset's actions are normalized separately and coordinate frames are not aligned, so an output is de-normalized differently per embodiment and the same vector can induce very different motions.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
question: In ACT's temporal ensemble, you lower m from 0.5 to 0.01. What changes?
options: Only the oldest prediction is used
Weights become nearly equal, so newer predictions count about as much as old ones and new observations are incorporated faster
The ensemble becomes a median instead of a mean
The policy is queried less often
explain: With m near 0, exp(-m i) is close to 1 for every i, so all predictions are averaged almost equally. The ACT paper states that a smaller m means faster incorporation of new observations.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Codebook collapse: measuring and fixing unused codes
question: Why does a dead code stay dead under the plain VQ-VAE codebook loss?
options: Its gradient is clipped by the commitment term
It receives gradient only when it is the nearest code to some encoder output, which it never is
The straight-through estimator sends it the wrong sign
Its distance is always zero
explain: The codebook term only involves the chosen code e_k. A code that never wins the argmin gets zero gradient, so it never moves toward the data and keeps losing.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction
question: A model has 32 attention layers that all use the same backend and one KV cache group. In one engine step, how many times does that backend's metadata builder run `build()`?
options: Once, and all 32 layers reuse the result
32 times, once per layer, because each layer has its own KV cache
Once per request in the batch
Zero times on decode steps, because decode metadata is cached
explain: The builder runs once per step per KV cache group, and the layers in that group share the metadata object. Per-layer work happens in `AttentionImpl.forward`. That is why `forward` must stay cheap on the CPU.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: Inside FLASH_ATTN's forward: from slot_mapping to one kernel call
question: Row 6 of the 14-token batch belongs to which request, and at which absolute position?
options: D, position 35
D, position 6
E, position 60
D, position 36
explain: cu_seqlens_q = [0, 1, 2, 3, 8, 14], and 3 <= 6 < 8, so it is request 3, D. D's 5 new tokens start at 37 - 5 = 32, and row 6 is D's fourth new row (offset 3), so its position is 35 and its slot is 3 x 16 + 3 = 51.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Turning an image into tokens a language model can read
question: Why does LLaVA feed the language model the patch grid rather than CLIP's single pooled image embedding?
options: The pooled embedding is not differentiable
The language model requires exactly 576 inputs
CLIP's pooled embedding is in the wrong numeric format
A single vector cannot hold fine details such as which number sits on which line, while a grid keeps local information
explain: A pooled vector summarizes the whole image, which works for retrieval. Reading and answering questions needs local detail, so LLaVA keeps one vector per patch. The token count is a design choice, not a requirement of the language model.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: Where VLMs fail and how they are evaluated
question: Your receipt extractor scores well on DocVQA-style questions but often miscounts the number of line items on long receipts. What is the most effective fix?
options: Ask the model to count more carefully
Switch to detail low to reduce noise
Do not rely on the model's count: extract the item list and count it in code, and validate against the printed subtotal
Report the DocVQA score instead
explain: Counting is a documented weakness. Turning the count into an extraction task (list every item) and doing the arithmetic in code removes the weak step and gives you a checksum.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: Making wait-free fast: fast path, slow path, and when to bother
question: In a fast-path-slow-path queue, the fast path is only lock-free. Why is each operation still wait-free?
options: Because the fast path is tried at most MAX_FAILURES times, and the slow path completes in a bounded number of steps thanks to helping
Because the fast path almost always succeeds in practice
Because fast and slow paths cannot run at the same time
Because MAX_FAILURES is set to the number of threads
explain: Wait-freedom is a worst-case property. The bound comes from capping the fast-path attempts and then relying on the wait-free slow path, whose bound comes from helping. It does not depend on the fast path usually succeeding, and the paper explicitly lets both paths run in parallel.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Inside the models: a multimesh GNN and a 3D Earth transformer
question: Pangu-Weather learns a different positional bias for windows at different latitudes. What assumption of a standard vision transformer does this remove?
options: That tokens must be square
That the same relative offset means the same thing everywhere in the image
That attention must be causal
That the number of channels is fixed
explain: Swin shares one relative-position bias across all windows, which suits translation-invariant images. On a lat-lon grid, one cell step spans a different distance and climate regime depending on latitude, so the bias is made position-specific.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: OWASP WSTG as a checklist you can prove you followed
question: A client asks why your report lists 'WSTG-BUSL-01 not tested on the refund workflow'. What is the best reason for including that line?
options: WSTG requires every test to appear in every report
Business logic tests cannot be performed by people
It honestly records a coverage gap so the client knows the refund logic is unassessed
It raises the overall severity of the report
explain: Listing what was not tested is part of an honest report (WSTG's Limitations section). Business logic is exactly what scanners miss, so the client needs to know that this workflow carries unassessed risk.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Beyond port 443: what FTP, SMB, SNMP, LDAP and SMTP give away
question: Why is `smtp-enum-users` tagged intrusive while `smtp-commands` is tagged safe?
options: smtp-enum-users uses a different port
smtp-commands needs a password
smtp-enum-users sends many guesses for user names, while smtp-commands only asks the server what it supports
Intrusive scripts are newer
explain: smtp-commands sends EHLO and HELP, normal client behaviour. smtp-enum-users issues VRFY, EXPN or RCPT for a list of names, generating load and looking like an attack, so Nmap tags it intrusive.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: File inclusion: when a path parameter chooses the code that runs
question: A page uses `include 'views/' . $name . '.php'` and the tester can reach `views/../admin/helpers.php`. Why is this worse than reading that file?
options: It is not worse; reading and including are equivalent
Include only works on files in the views folder
Include executes the file's PHP code inside the page, so any reachable PHP file, or uploaded content, runs
The .php suffix prevents any traversal
explain: Inclusion executes code. Reaching other PHP files can trigger their side effects, and combined with a way to plant a file, it becomes arbitrary code execution. The appended suffix narrows which files match but does not stop traversal.

courseTitle: Web application testing and bug bounty practice
lessonTitle: Case: Uber 2016, when a bug bounty was used to hide a breach
question: A person emails a company: 'I downloaded your customer table. Pay me through your bug bounty and I will delete it.' Under the Ninth Circuit's reasoning, would paying them through the bounty make their access authorised?
options: Yes, bounty payments create authorisation
Only if they sign an NDA
No; authorisation is assessed at the moment of access, and post hoc approval cannot launder it
Only if the data is deleted
explain: The court held that authorisation is judged at the time of access and that Uber's post hoc NDA could not retroactively authorise the hackers. This is extortion and a breach, to be handled by incident response and legal.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Origins and sites: how the browser names who owns a page
question: Is `https://app.example.com:8443` same-origin with `https://app.example.com`, and is it same-site?
options: Same-origin but cross-site
Cross-origin and cross-site
Same-origin and same-site
Cross-origin but same-site
explain: The ports differ (8443 vs the default 443), so the origins differ. A site is the scheme plus registrable domain and ignores ports, so both are the site https://example.com.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: CORS: how a server opts in to cross-origin reads
question: A preflight response includes `Access-Control-Max-Age: 600`. What does that do?
options: The browser may reuse this preflight's answer for up to 600 seconds instead of sending a new OPTIONS request
The server will reject requests older than 600 seconds
The real response may be cached by the browser for 600 seconds
The cookie set by the response expires after 600 seconds
explain: Access-Control-Max-Age only controls how long the result of the preflight (the allowed methods and headers) may be cached, subject to each browser's own maximum. It does not affect caching of the real response or any cookie.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Frames and clickjacking: X-Frame-Options and frame-ancestors
question: A developer adds `<meta http-equiv="X-Frame-Options" content="deny">` to the page HTML. Is the page now protected from clickjacking?
options: No, because DENY must be uppercase
No; X-Frame-Options is only honoured as an HTTP response header
Yes, but only in Chrome
Yes, meta tags are equivalent to headers
explain: MDN states that setting X-Frame-Options in a meta element has no effect. The same goes for frame-ancestors, which is not supported in meta. Both must be sent as real response headers.

courseTitle: The browser security model
lessonTitle: Site isolation: separate processes as a second wall
question: Which threat does Site Isolation address that the same-origin policy alone cannot?
options: A CSRF attack using a hidden form
A session cookie sent over HTTP
A malicious page reading another site's data from shared process memory via Spectre
A stored XSS bug in your own site
explain: Spectre lets script read memory in its own process without any software bug, so SOP checks never get a chance to refuse. Putting each site in its own process means that memory simply is not there to read. XSS, CSRF and cookie leaks are web-level bugs that site isolation does not change.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Accounts, groups and SIDs: how Windows names every identity
question: An admin renames the built-in Administrator account to `support` to hide it from attackers. Why does this give little protection?
options: Renaming is undone at every reboot
The account keeps RID 500 in its SID, and tools can look up accounts by SID
Windows refuses to rename that account
Attackers only ever guess the name Guest
explain: Microsoft notes a renamed Administrator keeps the same SID ending in 500, which attackers can discover. Disabling the account and using LAPS for local admin passwords are the real defences.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Processes, services and svchost: what runs, and as whom
question: A new service appears on a file server: name `UpdSvc`, account LocalSystem, path `C:\Users\Public\u.exe`, and a 7045 event from 02:14. Which detail is the strongest red flag?
options: It runs as LocalSystem
Its binary sits in a user-writable public folder rather than Program Files or System32
Its name is short
It was logged in the System log
explain: Many legitimate services run as LocalSystem. A SYSTEM service whose binary lives in a folder any user can write combines the service persistence trick with the writable-binary bug from the last lesson.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Event IDs that tell an intrusion story: 4688, 4720, 7045, 1102
question: An attacker clears the Security log on a server. What does a defender who only looks at that server's Security log afterwards see?
options: Nothing at all, so the attack is invisible
A 1102 event recording that the log was cleared, and only events written after it
Every old event, because clearing is undone at reboot
A 4720 event
explain: Clearing writes 1102, so the clear itself is visible. The older events are gone locally, which is why forwarding to a central collector matters.

courseTitle: Windows for security: accounts, processes, registry and event logs
lessonTitle: Remote Desktop and BlueKeep: logons before login
question: Which Security log entry is the normal record of a successful Remote Desktop sign-in?
options: 4624 with logon type 2
4624 with logon type 10
explain: Logon type 10 is RemoteInteractive: Terminal Services or Remote Desktop. Type 2 is a sign-in at the machine's own console.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WEP: how a 24-bit IV broke Wi-Fi's first encryption
question: A vendor offers 'WEP-256' with a 232-bit secret key. Does this fix WEP?
options: Partly: it fixes IV reuse but not bit flipping
No: the 24-bit IV still repeats, CRC-32 is still linear, and the key-schedule attacks still apply
Yes, as long as the IV is random
Yes, the key is now too long to brute force
explain: None of WEP's three structural flaws depend on the key length. NIST SP 800-97 says exactly this about longer WEP keys.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: WPA3: SAE, protected management frames and Enhanced Open
question: An airport switches its open Wi-Fi to OWE (Enhanced Open). Which threat does this remove?
options: Passive eavesdroppers reading other passengers' unencrypted traffic
Phishing pages on the captive portal
All man-in-the-middle attacks
An attacker running a fake 'Airport-Free' access point
explain: OWE gives each client its own keys from an unauthenticated Diffie-Hellman exchange, which defeats passive listening. With no authentication, a client cannot tell the real AP from a fake one.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Bluetooth and BLE: pairing, KNOB and BlueBorne
question: A smart lock pairs with phones using BLE Legacy Pairing in Just Works mode. What can a passive eavesdropper who records the pairing do?
options: Nothing, BLE is always encrypted
Derive the keys, because Legacy Just Works uses an all-zero temporary key
Only learn the lock's name
Cause the lock to require Numeric Comparison
explain: NIST SP 800-121: in LE Legacy Pairing Just Works, the temporary key is zero, so an eavesdropper does not need to guess it. LE Secure Connections uses ECDH, which defeats passive eavesdroppers.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Mobile app storage: secrets on disk and in the package
question: A banking app stores its refresh token in SharedPreferences with MODE_PRIVATE. The developer argues other apps cannot read it. Which threat does the argument miss?
options: Other apps on the same device
Backups, forensic extraction of a lost device, and malware with root, all of which can read the app's private files
The Play Store
Network attackers
explain: The UID sandbox does stop other apps. It does not stop someone who obtains the files by other routes. MASWE-0001 covers exactly this: sensitive data unencrypted in private storage.

courseTitle: Wireless and mobile security
lessonTitle: Lockdown Mode, stalkerware and tracker abuse
question: Which Lockdown Mode restriction most directly targets the zero-click entry points from lesson 17?
options: Most message attachment types are blocked and link previews are off, removing automatic parsing of attacker-sent content
Game Center is disabled
Location is removed from shared photos
Shared albums are removed
explain: FORCEDENTRY and Triangulation both entered through iMessage attachments parsed automatically. Blocking most attachment types and previews removes those parsers from the attack surface; the other restrictions serve privacy or other channels.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Production run queues: fixed rings, steal half, a LIFO slot
question: A Tokio worker's local queue is full (256 tasks) when it schedules one more. What happens?
options: The ring doubles to 512 slots
The new task waits until a slot frees up
128 queued tasks plus the new one, 129 in total, move to the global queue
Only the new task goes to the global queue, always
explain: Tokio never grows the ring. push_overflow claims the whole queue with one CAS, keeps the older 128 tasks locally and links the newer 128, plus the new task, into the mutex-protected global queue in one batch. (If a steal is already in progress the new task alone goes to the global queue, since the steal will free space.)

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Why the loss plunges during the decay: the river valley picture
question: In the river valley picture, why is the loss during the stable stage a bad indicator of how good the model will be after cooldown?
options: Because the validation set changes between stages
Because the high LR keeps the hill component elevated, hiding river progress that the decay will reveal
Because the stable stage only learns embeddings
Because the loss is computed with dropout on during the stable stage
explain: Loss = river + hill. A high LR inflates the hill part through bouncing between steep walls, so the plateau mostly reflects noise level, not lack of progress. The decay removes the hill part and the accumulated river progress shows up.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Cheap scaling studies, continual training and failure modes
question: Your team knows the exact token budget for a one-off production run and will never extend it. Which statement best matches the evidence?
options: With a known budget, a well-tuned decay over the whole run (for example linear to zero) can match or slightly beat WSD; WSD's main advantage is flexibility
WSD is strictly required, because cosine cannot reach the same loss
WSD is always at least 10% better in loss
Any schedule is fine as long as there is warmup
explain: Hägele et al. found cooldowns roughly match tuned cosine, and Bergsma et al. found linear decay-to-zero about 0.84% better than WSD at 80 tokens per parameter. WSD shines when the end date is uncertain or many lengths are needed.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: splice and tee: pipes as buffers of page references
question: Which call fails with EINVAL?
options: splice(file_fd, &off, pipe_w, NULL, n, 0)
splice(sock_fd, NULL, pipe_w, NULL, n, SPLICE_F_NONBLOCK)
tee(pipe1_r, pipe2_w, n, 0)
splice(file_fd, &off, sock_fd, NULL, n, 0)
explain: splice requires that at least one side is a pipe; file to socket has none, so it returns EINVAL. For file to socket use sendfile, which builds the internal pipe for you. The other three each involve a pipe on the correct side.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Embedding similarity with label descriptions
question: For T1 with descriptions, raising the softmax scale from 20 to 100 changes complaint's probability from 0.978 to about 1.0. What happens to accuracy?
options: It rises, because the model is more confident
It falls, because the model becomes overconfident
It does not change: scaling all cosines by the same factor keeps the ranking, so the argmax is identical
It depends on the embedding dimension
explain: Multiplying every cosine by the same positive number preserves their order, so the top label is unchanged for every input. Only the reported confidence changes, which is why softmax outputs from a hand-picked scale should not be read as calibrated probabilities.
